Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish.
